speaker: Professor
text: Ha, sorry to hear it. Okay, today we're covering hash tables, which build directly on last week's arrays.

speaker: Professor
text: Let's start with a definition. A hash function is a function that maps a key of arbitrary size to a fixed-size integer, which we use as an index into an array of buckets.

speaker: Professor
text: The important property is that the same key always produces the same index, and different keys should spread out evenly.

speaker: Professor
text: When two keys land in the same bucket, there are two main ways to handle it.

speaker: Professor
text: The first is separate chaining, where each bucket holds a linked list of entries.

speaker: Professor
text: The second is open addressing, where you probe for the next free slot, for example with linear probing.

speaker: Professor
text: Pay attention to this next part, because this will be on the exam: the difference between chaining and open addressing, and when you'd pick each.

speaker: Student
text: Is it okay if we just memorize the definitions?

speaker: Professor
text: Definitions won't be enough, you'll need to explain the trade-off. Chaining degrades gracefully, open addressing has better cache behavior.

speaker: Professor
text: Now, the load factor, which you saw in the reading for today.

speaker: Professor
text: When the load factor gets too high, around zero point seven five for open addressing, you resize and rehash everything.

speaker: Professor
text: And again, this will be on the exam: computing the amortized cost of insertion when the table doubles in size.

speaker: Professor
text: As a side note, my old advisor used to say hash tables are the duct tape of computer science. Not on the exam, just a nice line.

text: For homework, implement a hash table with separate chaining in the language of your choice, with insert, lookup and delete.
